prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B019, credited to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the scientific case. No member disputes the merit or maturity of the incretin chain, from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing through the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its insulinotropic and satiety actions to drugs with confirmed glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. The only live question is credit. I think the cleanest answer is a citation that rewards the physiology and the identity of the active hormone, which is a discovery in the sense the prize was written for, with the existence of the therapies stated as the consequence and not as a separately credited achievement. Holst, Drucker and Mojsov are the three contributions I can separate and defend, and all of them concern what the hormone is and does.
statement.case_against: The credit remains imperfect and I would rather say so in the record than hide it. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested and none of us can verify it against primary sources from the supplied material, Habener is outside the credited list, and leaving out Knudsen leaves unrewarded the acylation and albumin-binding step that produced a once-daily or once-weekly drug. A physiology-only citation can be read as understating why this became a medicine. I accept that cost. The alternative of crediting the drug step inside the same trio means dropping a physiological contributor to make room, which I find harder to justify than the omission. The caveat on Habener and Knudsen should be recorded, not used as grounds to defer a case that is otherwise mature.

responses.point: Linnarsson keeps Knudsen in the trio because acylation and albumin binding turned a minutes-long peptide into a drug and was a discovery in its own right, and says he would not block Mojsov under a purely physiological citation if her priority is discussed openly.
responses.response: That concession is what I think settles the third name. We have the same core, Drucker and Holst, and we differ on what the citation rewards. If the citation rests on physiology and the active peptide, Mojsov belongs in the trio and your own stated position does not oppose it. I do not call Knudsen's work routine. Half-life extension by fatty-acid acylation is real inventive science, and I have not changed my view that it is substantial. But it is a step downstream of the discovery of what the peptide is and does, and her contribution is the one thing in the trio that is not otherwise represented. I would also point out that your own case against B019 raises the Habener question, which cuts against Mojsov only if we treat her priority as unsettled, and then it argues for a clear caveat and not for replacing her with a different kind of contribution. I remain open to the second-part route you mention, but it would require removing a GLP-1 name, and I do not see a candidate good enough to justify that.

responses.point: Perlmann prefers the same trio, says he would revisit if diligence on Mojsov's priority proves unfavourable, and names B028 (Walter and Mori) as the cleaner two-person fallback because it has no comparable credit dispute.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your fallback and I have moved toward it. In round 1 I kept optogenetics as my first alternative. Your point, and the repeated objections from Linnarsson, Sandberg and Svenningsson about six claimants and the blend of channel discovery and neuronal application, have persuaded me that B016 cannot be defended with a three-person trio this year, so I now list B028 in its place. I would still ask the committee to be precise about what a failed Mojsov diligence would mean. If her priority were shown to be clearly secondary, I would not simply add Knudsen. I would then ask whether the part should be Holst and Drucker alone, which leaves the citation honest, or whether a second part is justified. I would not let uncertainty that nobody here can resolve decide the outcome in advance.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, asks whether the B019 citation should cover only physiology and the active peptide or also therapy, and whether a second part is warranted given that the three-person limit applies to the union of names.
responses.response: My answer is physiology and the active peptide, with the therapeutic consequence in the citation as the reason it matters, and no second part this year. A second part under the union limit would force at least one of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov out to admit two people from B014 or B028, and each of those is a serious achievement that I would not want to see paired with a damaged B019. I also do not think pairing is needed to make the prize strong. Your own framing of the citation around the active form of the hormone is the one I would adopt, and I would accept your wording almost unchanged. I disagree, mildly, that Habener's absence argues for changing the configuration. It argues for a footnote on the record, because we cannot add a name that is not on the credited list without leaving the supplied evidence.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius says she would not discount Mojsov because her credit is contested, since identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form was a necessary step, and offers B014 or B032 as clearly attributable alternatives if the GLP-1 attribution is judged unresolvable.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of Mojsov and with the principle that a contested history is a reason to read the record, not to drop a name. On the fallbacks, I would now rank B014 above B032 and I would not offer B032 as an alternative. My round-1 doubt about TNF blockade was originality and I have not been given reason to change it. The step from concept to validated target is clear, but it is the demonstration of benefit that is credited, and that makes it a weaker candidate than B014, where the engineered receptor and its clinical proof are both discoveries. For B014 I would keep the pair June and Sadelain and not take up Rosenberg, for the reason you give that I cannot find a non-arbitrary way to include him. Eshhar remains a real gap that I would want recorded if B014 is ever advanced.

responses.point: Sandberg builds the B019 prize on Holst for physiology, Mojsov for the active peptide and Drucker for GLP-1 biology and translation, and asks whether a second part such as B028 would strengthen or dilute a prize already strong on B019.
responses.response: I think a second part would dilute it, and I say this as someone who rates the unfolded protein response highly as a discovery. B028 is a clean two-person credit and a conceptually original finding, but its therapeutic consequences are still emerging, as Perlmann and Wahren-Herlenius say, and attaching it under the union limit costs a GLP-1 name. That trades a complete chain for two incomplete ones. I also take your point on the research-tool status of optogenetics, which I had underweighted when ranking it second. Where I differ from you is on the weight of the drug step. You say excluding the drug developers risks citing physiology while the clinical impact came from engineering. I think that risk is real but is answered by wording the citation so that the therapies appear as the consequence of the discovery, which is both accurate and consistent with how earlier physiology prizes were framed.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is secure enough to hold a place among three, given Habener's absence from the credited list, none of us having checked primary sources
Whether wording the citation around physiology and the active peptide, with therapy as consequence, will be read as fair to Knudsen's acylated analogues
Whether the committee would accept a Drucker and Holst only configuration if the Mojsov question turned unfavourable, and what that would do to the strength of the prize
How much weight the still-accumulating long-term safety and outcome data should carry, which I do not treat as a reason to delay
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure and nothing new arises from round 1. My profile documents no co-authorship or other tie to any credited name on the shortlist, including Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, June, Sadelain, Walter or Mori. My documented connections to Grillner, Ernfors and Perlmann (a 2009 paper on stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons) do not involve the incretin candidates. I use optogenetics as a research tool, which is not a tie to any credited name, and since I no longer treat B016 as my main alternative this is even less relevant. I do not request recusal.
